title: World Organ Donation Day: Six Myths About Kidney Donation That Persist in India
excerpt: With over 2 lakh Indians awaiting kidney transplants each year, doctors say misconceptions around donation — not a shortage of willing donors — remain the biggest barrier.
body:
• India needs over 2 lakh kidney transplants annually, but only about 10,000 patients receive one — a gap driven largely by myths and low awareness rather than a shortage of potential donors.
  • India's cadaver organ donation rate is less than one per million population, compared to 70-80% deceased donation rates in Western countries.
  • Nephrologists say living donors can lead completely normal lives after donating a kidney, including playing sports and returning to work within 2-3 months.
  • Religious misconceptions — such as the belief that donating an organ means being born without it in the next life — remain a major barrier across India and the diaspora.

A Gap That Costs Lives

Every day, 17 patients in India die waiting for an organ donor. The country performs the second largest number of transplants globally, yet its cadaver organ donation rate — less than one donor per million population per year — ranks among the world's lowest. Western countries, by contrast, achieve deceased donation rates of 70-80%.

On World Organ Donation Day, observed annually on August 13, nephrologists and transplant surgeons across India renewed calls to dismantle the myths that keep those numbers low.

"India faces a severe organ wastage crisis, losing approximately 2 lakh kidneys and other vital organs annually due to a lack of awareness, deep-rooted superstitions, and myths surrounding brain death," said Dr. Tanima Das Bhattacharya, consultant nephrologist at Narayana Health, Kolkata.

The Six Myths

Myth 1: Donors can't live a normal life. Nephrologists consistently say this is the most damaging misconception. A healthy person can lead a completely normal life with one kidney. Most living kidney donors return to work within two to three months and face no long-term restrictions on physical activity, including sports. Regular follow-up, hydration, and a healthy lifestyle are the main requirements.

Myth 2: You can't play sports with one kidney. Dr. Anupam Roy, a nephrologist at Hindustan Times' health series, addressed this directly: living donors who pass comprehensive medical evaluations can resume full physical activity. Professional athletes have competed at high levels after kidney donation.

Myth 3: Organ donation goes against religious beliefs. Multiple religious leaders and scholars across Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, and Sikhism have affirmed that organ donation is consistent with — and often encouraged by — their faiths. Yet the belief that donating an organ means being "born without it in the next life" persists in many communities.

"In India, people are not willing to donate blood, forget organ donations. Among multiple factors behind low awareness are religious beliefs that prohibit organ donation."

— Dr. Vivek Gupta, Senior Consultant, Liver Transplantation, Medanta Hospital, Lucknow

Myth 4: Anyone can donate to anyone. Indian law strictly regulates who can donate. Under the Human Organ Transplantation Act (HOTA, 1994), only first-degree relatives — grandparents, parents, siblings, spouses, and children — are typically eligible as living donors. Buying or selling organs is illegal and punishable under the law.

Myth 5: Hospitals let patients die to harvest organs. Dr. Pragnesh Desai of Yatharth Super Speciality Hospital said doctors always prioritize saving a patient's life first. Organ donation is considered only after brain death is declared following stringent medical and legal protocols. Multiple independent doctors must confirm brain death before any organ retrieval can proceed.

Myth 6: Older people can't be donors. There is no fixed upper age limit for organ donation. Suitability depends on the individual's overall health rather than age. Comprehensive medical, laboratory, and imaging assessments determine whether a donor is fit, regardless of their age.

The Diaspora Connection

These myths don't stop at India's borders. Cultural misconceptions often travel with immigrant families, and Indian-American and NRI communities frequently carry the same hesitations about organ donation. In the United States, South Asians are among the fastest-growing groups on transplant waiting lists, partly due to higher rates of diabetes and hypertension — yet donor registration rates remain low.

Registering as an organ donor in the US, UK, or Canada is straightforward and can be done through national registries or at the time of driver's license renewal.

A Single Donor, Multiple Lives

A single deceased donor can save up to eight lives through organ donation and improve 50 more through tissue donation — corneas, skin, bone, heart valves, and tendons. For the 2 lakh Indians awaiting a kidney transplant each year, the math is clear: the gap is not one of science or logistics but of awareness and willingness.
